theme_note: Participants turn invitations into actionable pixel work by locating targets, recruiting people, assigning roles, publishing plans, refreshing live information and arranging watches; what varies is whether the work is a flag, an EU image, or the practical mechanics of reaching it.

Participants protect a shared drawing by reporting threats, setting watches, prioritising maintainable borders, withholding pixels from attacks, and pushing an encroaching image away; tactics and targets vary while maintenance holds the codes together.

Participants make anti-swastika work part of the flag project by locating, dismantling and overpainting symbols and celebrating computer-based anti-fascism; the codes vary between direct action, enabling terrain and moral framing.

second_order: claiming German and European belonging together
theme_note: Participants answer national flag work by naming European identity, asking to hold both identities, or condemning attacks on European neighbours; the variation is accommodation versus moral criticism.

Participants propose, accept, refuse and invoke bargains about Austrian lettering, French borders and Touhou artwork; what varies is the neighbour and whether the offer is accepted, late or invoked as an obligation.

second_order: expanding and boasting about German space
theme_note: Participants frame growth as conquest, domination or eastward expansion, direct pixels into neighbouring space and puncture or joke about those boasts; what varies is operational expansion versus ironic or critical commentary on it.
A participant places pixels while drinking and listening to music, making event participation one activity within an ordinary evening; this single-code practice belongs with no other early group.

second_order: performing and judging April Fools jokes
theme_note: Participants stage, recognise, fall for, praise, reject and complain about the room’s own April Fools tricks, including clock checks, place-name puns, fake-news readings, recycled pranks and a Discord screenshot; the jokes vary but the shared practice is testing and evaluating dated deception, not canvas work.

Participants discover, request and provide access to r/de’s Discord through the sidebar while noting mobile access limits; the codes vary between asking, directing, thanking and questioning visibility.

Participants put forward recognisable images and named operations, revise them for available space, or reject embellishment as too hard to maintain; designs vary from eagles and hearts to European banners and peace operations.

second_order: watching, explaining and auditing the canvas
theme_note: Participants make the changing canvas legible by sharing maps, explaining the rules and group formation, judging scale and efficiency, reading visual details, or watching others work; the variation is live orientation versus reflective inspection.
Participants explicitly relocate attack, defence or general r/place coordination to Discord servers; what varies is the server and stated task, while the hidden decisions remain outside Reddit.

second_order: turning pixel conflict into arguments about nationalism
theme_note: Participants use canvas conflict to argue over imperialism, war memory, national pride and hostility toward France; the positions vary from mock-historical escalation to criticism of nationalism.
Participants claim pride in assisting an operation and celebrate that the collective accomplished it; this is achievement talk rather than the coordination or placement itself.

Moderators and participants concentrate separate event posts into a megathread or dedicated venue, while others contest whether one thread can coordinate the work; the practice varies between formal rule, official-project claim and practical redirection.

second_order: building with templates, scripts and bots
theme_note: Participants turn designs into repeatable pixel work through scripts, bots, spreadsheets and separate templates, including help for sleepers; the tools vary in automation and task while making distributed building reproducible.

Participants temporarily remake the subreddit as Delaware by welcoming the change, teaching state facts, parodying citizenship and local rivalry, carrying German traditions into it, and arguing over when the redesign should end; the shared practice is sustaining and contesting the room’s own fiction, separate from the canvas.

Participants resume the room’s ordinary recurring conversation, sharing an exam and encouragement while the same thread absorbs weekend event recollections; the ordinary exchange belongs with no canvas practice.

Participants turn shared time-lapse viewing into a distributed song by contributing successive words and mutating the chorus; the practice is playful call-and-answer rather than assessment of the canvas.

second_order: joking with visitors through food, flags and rivalry
theme_note: Participants answer outside approaches with chants, thanks, food corrections, sport and bodily boasts, or local jokes about saved carrot art; the visitors and joke objects vary while cordial rivalry holds the exchanges together.

second_order: marking and mourning the end of Place
theme_note: Participants announce that placement has ended, look back fondly, respond with relief or sadness, regret unfinished work and wish the action had lasted longer; reactions vary while all orient to closure.

second_order: debating whether Place pushed Reddit’s app
theme_note: Participants test the suspicion that r/place sought notification permission or official-app uptake by offering opt-out logic, firsthand app use, alternative clients, browser workarounds and mockery; the evidence and judgments remain disputed.

second_order: starting again on a successor canvas
theme_note: A participant points to a new canvas where a German flag has already begun; this single-code continuation belongs with no other post-event practice.

second_order: comparing repeated wall repainting with r/place
theme_note: Participants call restored wall art `r/place IRL`, compare manual repainting with scripts, interpret additions and argue over anarchy and tagging; the physical restoration cycle borrows event language without becoming canvas work.
